piaget-stages.def: Jean Piaget’s theory that children’s thinking develops through four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), each a qualitatively different way of understanding the world.

sensorimotor.def: Piaget’s first stage, from birth to about age 2, when infants learn about the world through their senses and actions and develop object permanence.

object-permanence.def: The understanding that objects continue to exist when they cannot be seen, heard or touched; it develops during the first year.

preoperational.def: Piaget’s second stage, from about 2 to 7, when children use words and images and play make-believe, but are egocentric and do not yet reason logically about changes such as pouring.

egocentrism.def: In Piaget’s theory, a young child’s difficulty taking another person’s point of view; it means seeing the world only from one’s own perspective, not selfishness.

conservation.def: The understanding that an amount (of liquid, number or mass) stays the same when its shape or arrangement changes; it usually develops in the concrete operational stage.

theory-of-mind.def: The understanding that other people have their own thoughts, feelings and beliefs, which can differ from one’s own and can be false; usually clear by age 4 to 5.

concrete-operational.def: Piaget’s third stage, from about 7 to 11, when children reason logically about concrete, real situations and understand conservation.

formal-operational.def: Piaget’s fourth stage, from about age 12, when people can reason about abstract ideas and hypothetical situations.

zpd.def: Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development: the range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with help from someone more skilled.

scaffolding.def: Temporary support (hints, steps, demonstrations) from a more skilled person that helps a learner in the zone of proximal development, removed as skill grows.

crystallized.def: Crystallized intelligence: accumulated knowledge and skills such as vocabulary and facts; it holds steady or grows into later adulthood.

fluid.def: Fluid intelligence: the ability to reason quickly and solve new problems; it tends to decline gradually from early adulthood.

dementia.def: A decline in memory and thinking severe enough to interfere with daily life, caused by brain disease (most often Alzheimer’s disease); it is not a normal part of aging.
